content.p: Maragha was one of the larger Armenian villages of northeastern Nagorno-Karabakh. On 10 April 1992, in the middle of the first war over the region, Azerbaijani forces attacked it with shelling, armour and infantry. Armenian accounts say that dozens of villagers who had stayed behind, many of them elderly or disabled, were killed, and that many more were taken away as hostages. The village was later occupied by Azerbaijani forces and has been outside Armenian control since.

What is known of the day comes chiefly from Armenian officials, Armenian news outlets, a Christian advocacy group and a few visitors. They agree on the outline and disagree on the numbers. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International are cited for the core claims, but as quoted or summarised by those outlets. Azerbaijan's own account is not set out here, and nothing in this account is a court finding.
content.h2: A large village on the front line
content.p: Before the war Maragha was, by the Armenian Weekly's description, one of the largest and richest villages in Karabakh, with several factories and a developed wine-growing trade. It lay in the Martakert district just across the line from the Azerbaijani town of Terter (Mir-Bashir). From 1954 it and the nearby village of Margushevan were joined in one state farm named Leninavan.

The 1989 census counted more than 5,000 people, according to the Armenian Weekly. Most were ethnic Armenians, together with a few families who had fled pogroms in Sumgait, Baku and other parts of Soviet Azerbaijan. By spring 1992 Azerbaijan had blockaded Nagorno-Karabakh for about two years, in the words of the Armenian accounts, and the border villages were being raided and shelled. Many residents had already left, some resettling elsewhere in Karabakh. Those who stayed organised self-defence units from locals of Maragha and nearby villages, which set up four positions around the settlement while residents dug underground shelters.

According to the unit's commander, Roma Karapetyan, the first attack came on 25 and 26 February 1992 and was beaten back. In April, he said, the offensives began to be directed by forces of the Azerbaijani Defense Ministry.

Accounts of the day come from the Armenian side. The Armenian Weekly says units of the Azerbaijani Defense Ministry, Internal Affairs Ministry and OMON special police attacked three times without success before the main assault, which used many armoured vehicles including tanks. The Armenian Report describes artillery fire followed by a ground assault, with tanks entering by the afternoon, followed by infantry and looters. The Armenian Weekly says Human Rights Watch (Helsinki Watch) interviewed an eyewitness who took part in the defence, and that the defenders had to retreat because they lacked equipment for a counter-attack.

According to the Armenian Report, the villagers fled their homes while those who remained, mainly elderly and disabled people, sought refuge in basements and underground shelters. The Armenian Weekly says about 118 civilians who could not leave were attacked, and that within five to six hours about 50 were killed while almost as many were taken hostage.

Karapetyan's recollection of the Armenian counter-attack is stark. He said that in the streets he saw one in ten people with swords, and that he ordered his men to shoot those carrying them. He said the plan was to retake the village before dawn, because the longer they waited the more civilians would be tortured, and that they found bodies of civilians marked with crosses cut by swords. He claimed that Azerbaijan lost 44 men and the Armenian side none. The Armenian Weekly adds that two volunteers who joined the relief group, Leonig Azgaldyan and Vladimir Balayan, received the Artsakh Hero title posthumously in 2019. The pages give no single timeline for the end of the assault. Karapetyan describes a counter-attack planned for before dawn, while Christian Solidarity International says, quoting the World Evangelical Alliance, that its team arrived a day after the Azerbaijani troops had withdrawn.

Cox said that she and a team from Christian Solidarity arrived within hours and found "homes still smoldering, decapitated corpses, charred human remains, and survivors in shock." The Armenian Report describes decapitations, mutilations and the burning of bodies. The Armenian Weekly relays eyewitness accounts of people dragged behind a tank, burned alive or mutilated. These descriptions are testimony quoted by Armenian outlets, not findings by a court.

The Armenian Weekly quotes Amnesty International as reporting that over 100 residents were "slain, while their bodies were profaned and disfigured", and that two weeks later the village was attacked again, its population deported, and houses pillaged and then mostly burned. The original Amnesty text was not available to check.
content.h2: How many died, and how many were taken
content.p: The counts do not match and are listed here with whoever gave them.

For the dead, the Armenian foreign ministry and the Armenian Weekly say more than 50 or about 50 people, the ministry specifying more than 50 civilians including 30 women. The World Evangelical Alliance, speaking at the UN Human Rights Council in September 2022, said 45 Armenian Christians. The Armenian Weekly quotes Amnesty as saying over 100 residents were slain, and the Armenian Report repeats a figure of more than 100 tortured and killed.

For hostages, the foreign ministry says 29 women and 9 children, and the fate of 19 is still unknown. The Armenian Weekly says almost as many hostages as dead, among them 29 women, nine children and disabled people, adding that some were later rescued, including all of the children, while 19 remain unaccounted for. The Armenian Report says 53 were taken, 19 of whom were never returned. The World Evangelical Alliance said over 50.

The Armenian Weekly records one hostage's account. Karine Poghosyan said she was taken with her two infants and her father-in-law, and that captors cursed them as Armenians. Her daughter was later found in an orphanage in Azerbaijan, silent, and began to speak Azerbaijani words after a few days. After the exchange the child was scared at the sight of soldiers or cars.

The Armenian Weekly says a second, much larger offensive began in May 1992, aimed at Stepanakert, with Maragha and Margushevan among its targets. Armenian units fought from 10 May to the end of June, it says, but lacking armoured vehicles they could not hold, and Azerbaijan occupied both villages at the end of June 1992. The Armenian Report says the village is under Azerbaijani control and that former residents are scattered across Russia, Armenia and other parts of Nagorno-Karabakh. It says survivors established a new village, Nor Maraga, in Karabakh, where a monument stands to the victims.

No Azerbaijani trial for the killings is reported. The Armenian Report says the perpetrators have never been held accountable. The Armenian Weekly goes further: it asserts that Azerbaijan has never been held accountable and that members of the units involved were later made National Heroes of Azerbaijan. That is the Armenian Weekly's assertion and is not corroborated here by any Azerbaijani account.

Armenian officials have used the anniversary to argue about impunity. In 2017, on the 25th anniversary, Deputy Foreign Minister Shavarsh Kocharyan said Azerbaijan had committed gross violations of international humanitarian law. He said OMON had burned the village and that the villagers were tortured to death, and that the lack of accountability encouraged later crimes, citing the April 2016 fighting. In 2025 the foreign ministry said Maragha's Armenians had been subjected to complete ethnic cleansing. It argued that preventing such atrocities required abandoning hate speech.

In 2022 the World Evangelical Alliance mentioned Maragha at the UN Human Rights Council and Christian Solidarity International's president, John Eibner, said that to accept Azerbaijani sovereignty over Nagorno-Karabakh would be to accept ethnic and religious cleansing.
The Armenian Report says international media coverage of the massacre remained sparse.
